feat(engine): pin a durable scheduled save-proof harness [W3-D18-02a] (#145)

Re-runnable save-proof harness with a readiness gate that verifies the runtime and config by hash, restricts the subject to A, caps the fee, enforces a one-hour proof window and refuses an unreconciled attempt. Adds tests pinning the two live-submit guards a mutation found unguarded, and fixes a /tmp assumption that made the harness unusable on macOS while CI stayed green.

fix(cli): scan grades against both tiers, not the action threshold alone (#154)

scan could never say WARNING because it graded against the action threshold alone, so it reported HEALTHY for an entry the engine called WARNING. Both tiers are now graded and printed; exit codes still use the action tier and are unchanged. Closes #150.

feat(engine): add explicit unavailable channel stubs [W3-D17-02] (#138)

WebhookChannel and TelegramChannel satisfy NotificationChannel and always reject with ChannelNotImplementedError, identifying delivery as SOW 2 scope. Neither takes constructor arguments, reads the record, touches the network or logs, so the refusal cannot drift into a partial implementation. Reconciled onto main after #137: both export sets kept, D17-01's completed tracking restored.

feat(ci): enforce timeout<interval; measure the real cadence [W3-D18-01] (#136)

THE PROSE RULE IS NOW A CHECK

`timeout-minutes` must be strictly less than the cron interval. With
cancel-in-progress:false a run queues rather than cancelling — correct, because
cancelling mid-submission is how an unresolved hash is created — but that is
only safe while runs finish faster than they arrive. Above the interval it
silently becomes an unbounded queue of transaction-submitting runs.

I found that yesterday and wrote it down. Prose does not fire; four payments and
counting. Commissioned three ways: timeout above interval fails, timeout EQUAL
to interval fails (strictly-less), and a scheduled workflow with no timeout at
all fails. An unparsed cron is reported rather than assumed safe.

W3-D18-01 — DEPLOYED, AND THE CADENCE IS NOT WHAT IT CLAIMS

ADR-003 chose GitHub Actions + Node 24, which is what engine-cron.yml already
is — so this row and W3-D18-00 converged on one deployment once the platform
decision landed. 12 scheduled runs, all success, genuinely unattended.

But:

  declared     3,18,33,48 * * * *   -> every 15 minutes
  expected     124 fires in the observed window
  ACTUAL        12                  -> 10% of schedule
  median gap   132 min    worst gap 294 min

GitHub throttles scheduled workflows on low-activity repos. Documented platform
behaviour, not a misconfiguration — but the file says 15 minutes and reality is
roughly two hours.

The row asks for "a real cron cadence (5-15 min)". We are NOT achieving that, so
it stays [~] rather than being claimed. Measured and published beats asserted
and quietly wrong.

Sufficient for the only deadline that cares: B's threshold-to-expiry is a
24-hour window, so even at the worst observed gap the engine fires 4-5 times
inside it. That margin comes from the TWO-TIER THRESHOLD, not the cadence —
17,280 ledgers is a full day of warning, which absorbs a scheduler missing 90%
of its slots. A tighter threshold would not have survived this.

Not "fixing" it: a keepalive games the platform to make a YAML number true, and
moving to Cloudflare six days before the crossing reopens a closed decision with
unresolved SDK compatibility.

SATURDAY PRE-FLIGHT, WRITTEN FOR FRIDAY

docs/SEP-20-PREFLIGHT.md. Names who watches and what they do if no scheduled run
appears between 12:00-14:00 UTC: dispatch by hand. Given a ~132 minute median
gap that is expected rather than exceptional.

Verifies check-crossing-evidence.mjs in BOTH directions — red before the commit,
green after — because a check that passes while blind to its subject looks
identical to one that passes correctly.

And states plainly that nobody "fixes" the refusal: it IS the evidence, and
anyone editing _doNotWatch or the guard to produce a save is destroying it.

W3-D21-01e DATED: WED SEP 24

Between B's expiry and C's. Late enough that there is something real to stand
up, early enough that findings are fixable inside Week 3. Until then nobody
walks Fatih through the engine — the resource is spent the first time anyone
explains anything, including in a PR description written to reassure.

docs(readme): a quickstart that works today, verified by running it [W3-D21-01c] (#133)

The previous quickstart was "*(Available once packages are published — W4-D27.)*"
plus an `npx` line that does not resolve yet. That is exactly the placeholder
this row warns about: W3-D21-01b's fresh-machine run against it would have
measured nothing and reported success.

Now it is the real front door — clone, install, build, scan our public test
contract. No key, no account, no signup, because scanning is a permissionless
read and nothing in the quickstart can spend anything.

EVERY COMMAND WAS RUN BEFORE IT WAS WRITTEN

  pnpm cli scan <A>                      exit 0
  ... --cost --ledgers 518400            exit 0
  ... --json / --optimize                exit 0
  scan A B C  (multi-contract)           exit 0
  extend --help                          exit 0
  bad contract id                        exit 2, as documented

The sample output is captured from those runs rather than invented, and the test
contract is deliberately long-lived so it reads the same for a stranger as it
did for us.

It leads with the thing a stranger cannot know: contracts built from one Wasm
share a single ContractCode entry, a single-contract scan CANNOT tell you
whether others depend on it, and `scan A B C` resolves it. Exit codes are
documented with the caveat that a clean exit means "everything I was asked to
check is healthy" and never "this contract is fully healthy".

ONE CLAIM CORRECTED BEFORE IT SHIPPED

I wrote that the shared entry is 98% of the rent bill, attached to the
three-contract example. That example measures 97% — the 98% figure belongs to a
single-contract scan with data keys. Attaching a number to the wrong scenario is
the crossesOn collision in miniature, so both are now stated with their scope.

feat(ci): enforce Sep 20 crossing capture; hunt the flake where it failed (#132)

TWO HOLES IN THE SEP 20 EVIDENCE CHAIN, BOTH IN WHAT I BUILT YESTERDAY

1. The artifact expires. `engine-run-…` is retained 90 days; the submission is
   2026-10-02. Fine for operations, wrong for evidence — an artifact is a log,
   a commit is evidence.

2. The same-day check could not fire for it. `check-evidence-hashes.mjs` was
   correctly narrowed to SUBMISSION outcomes, but Sep 20's evidence is a
   REFUSAL: no transaction, no hash, nothing for that check to verify. The
   mechanism enforcing same-day indexing was blind exactly where the week's
   least repeatable event lands.

Same shape as the original "a refusal leaves no trace" problem, one layer down:
we built the capture, and the verification of the capture still only looked for
transactions.

`scripts/check-crossing-evidence.mjs` is DATE-TRIGGERED. From each subject's
alertThresholdOn onward it fails `pnpm check` until a committed file under
docs/evidence/ carries that contract ID and a "REFUSED BY WRITE GUARD" line. It
cannot be forgotten on the day, because the day is when it starts failing — and
unlike a reminder, it keeps failing.

Commissioned across every boundary: Sep 19 passes, Sep 20 fails naming B and its
expiry, Sep 25 flags both B and C, and committing a matching file clears it.
Dates are READ from write-guard.ts rather than duplicated — moving a crossing
there moves the check with it, verified by mutation.

FLAKE HUNT ON THE MACHINE THAT FAILED

Of the three remaining hypotheses for #128 — I/O contention, runner cgroup
limits, a different Node build — all are properties of the CI runner and none
can be tested on a laptop. My 40-run local loop at 10-way saturation could not
have reproduced any of them.

So a manual workflow runs the same loop on a runner. It either reproduces, or it
converts the park from "not reproducible locally" into "not reproducible on the
machine that failed". It does not fail the job on a reproduction: the
reproduction IS the result, and a red job would read as broken CI.

A RULE

A substring assertion is a proxy, and proxies fail hardest near the requirement.
The `restore` test banned a word and rejected the correct sentence "It cannot be
restored" — because correct copy mentions a forbidden thing precisely in order
to rule it out. Distinct from the wrong-oracle and compound-clause rules: those
are a test encoding the wrong spec or never reaching its branch; this is a test
encoding the RIGHT spec through the wrong kind of evidence.

fix(ci): the engine cron failed silently and reported green (#118)

Two defects in #117, both mine, found by reading the first run instead of
trusting its green tick.

1. IT POINTED AT THE EXAMPLE CONFIG

`EVERGREEN_CONFIG: evergreen.config.example.json`, which carries deliberate
placeholder IDs that `loadConfig` correctly refuses. I built
`evergreen.config.dogfood.json` in the same PR and did not wire it.

2. THE STEP REPORTED SUCCESS WHILE THE SCRIPT DIED

`pnpm engine:run | tee /tmp/engine.log` with no `shell: bash`. GitHub's default
shell has no `pipefail`, so the step's exit code is TEE's — which always
succeeds. The run died on the config error above and the job went green.

That is a silent failure in the one job designed to run unattended, and it is
the same `$?`-after-a-pipe trap this repo has now hit repeatedly — including
once while verifying the work that produced this very runner. Knowing about a
trap is not the same as not falling into it, which is the argument for
`shell: bash` being in the file rather than in someone's memory.

Worth stating plainly: had this not been read, the cron would have reported
success every 15 minutes until ~Sep 20, when its silence would have been
indistinguishable from "the engine saw nothing".
